item.text:
Based on the supplied text, these are the drafting and enforcement vulnerabilities I would flag. Some omissions may be partly addressed by generally applicable law; they should not automatically be treated as eliminating existing federal authority.

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” invites fragmentation.** A developer could divide training among successive runs, checkpoints, fine-tuning stages, or cooperating models, each below the threshold. The bill supplies no aggregation or anti-circumvention rule.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** “Quantity of computing power” confuses a rate or capacity with a total operation count, and the text does not specify how to count integer operations, floating-point operations, mixed precision, sparsity, or specialized hardware. Different accounting methods could produce materially different coverage.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—The threshold excludes exactly \(10^{26}\) operations.** “Greater than” rather than “at least” leaves systems trained at precisely the threshold outside this prong. There is also no measurement-tolerance rule.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—A fixed compute threshold will become outdated.** Algorithmic and hardware improvements could enable increasingly capable systems below the threshold. There is no authority to update it; the capability-based prong would require a separate determination.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Nontraining compute is not clearly counted.** Inference-time reasoning, search, external tools, and other system-level computation could substantially increase capabilities without increasing the model’s counted training operations. Coverage would depend on the separately administered capability prong.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Coverage of derivative models is unclear.** The bill does not say whether a distilled, compressed, merged, or otherwise modified model inherits its predecessor’s training-compute history. Developers could argue that only the derivative’s own training counts.

7. **§ 2(1)—“Model” and “system” are used inconsistently.** Prong (A) covers a model while prong (B) covers a system, without defining either or specifying their relationship. This creates uncertainty about ensembles, agent networks, tool-using systems, and applications built around covered models.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is undefined.** The text never identifies which Secretary makes capability determinations. Commerce’s registry role and State’s negotiating role do not unambiguously resolve that assignment.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—The capability standard lacks objective criteria.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” and “most cognitive tasks” leave the magnitude, human comparison group, task universe, and measurement method unspecified. These ambiguities create enforcement disputes and fair-notice concerns, especially for criminal liability.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—Dangerous specialized systems may escape coverage.** A system could have extraordinary capabilities in strategically important domains without exceeding human performance across “most” cognitive tasks. If trained below the compute threshold, it would not necessarily qualify.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—Coverage depends on an affirmative determination.** The language appears to require the Secretary to act before this prong covers a system, allowing development or deployment while designation is pending. There is no determination deadline or interim restriction.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—No designation procedure is established.** The bill does not specify notice, evidentiary standards, testing procedures, effective dates, reconsideration, or treatment of updated versions. General administrative law may provide a framework, but these omissions invite delay and litigation over individual designations.

13. **§§ 2(1)(B), 4—No mandatory capability disclosure or testing.** Developers need not notify the government that a system may meet the capability standard, submit evaluation results, or provide access for testing. Facility workload reports are not an adequate substitute, particularly for systems developed outside covered facilities.

14. **§ 2(2)—“U.S. person” omits several important categories.** The definition excludes noncitizen permanent residents and does not clearly include LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated organizations, or entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those omissions matter particularly for conduct abroad.

15. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not automatically covered.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary of a U.S. company is not itself a “U.S. person” under this definition. A U.S. parent’s own prohibited conduct might still create liability, but ownership or control alone is not expressly enough.

16. **§ 3(a)—The location of remote conduct is unclear.** The bill does not specify whether training or deployment occurs where the actor, servers, controlling entity, or users are located. Cross-border cloud arrangements could exploit competing interpretations of “in the United States.”

17. **§ 3(a)—Foreign supply into the United States is not expressly addressed.** A foreign provider operating entirely abroad could argue that supplying API access or model weights to U.S. customers does not constitute its own deployment “in the United States.” The bill contains no separate import, distribution, or market-access restriction.

18. **§ 3(a)—“Train, develop, or deploy” is undefined.** It is unclear whether these terms include fine-tuning, hosting, licensing, releasing weights, integrating a model, or operating an already deployed system. Liability should not depend on uncertain interpretations of these verbs.

19. **§§ 2(1), 3(a)—Pre-threshold development creates a timing problem.** A developer could argue that work on a not-yet-covered system is lawful until it crosses the compute threshold or receives a capability designation. The bill does not clearly prohibit commencing a project expected to produce a covered system or specify when such a project must stop.

20. **§ 3(a)—Possession, transfer, and continued use are not expressly regulated.** Covered weights could be retained, sold, or transferred even if further training and deployment are prohibited. Whether continued operation or use constitutes “deploy[ment]” is left unresolved, and there is no affirmative shutdown or secure-custody requirement.

21. **§ 3(a)—Facilitation liability is not clearly specified.** The bill does not expressly address financing, procuring, directing, or knowingly providing compute for prohibited activity. Existing criminal aiding-and-abetting and conspiracy law may reach some conduct, but the text does not establish comparably clear civil liability or provider duties.

22. **§ 3(a)—Government application is uncertain.** “Any person” does not unmistakably establish how the prohibition applies to federal agencies, government laboratories, or sovereign entities. Contractor liability may differ from the government’s own liability, leaving important public-sector activity legally uncertain.

23. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering exempts systems, not merely existing training.** A covered system whose training began before enactment appears exempt from the entire prohibition indefinitely. That could permit completion, further development, and deployment of a grandfathered system regardless of its eventual capabilities.

24. **§ 3(b)—A token pre-enactment start could secure exemption.** “Training began” has no minimum-substance requirement or restriction on dormant projects. Companies could initiate numerous nominal runs before enactment and later claim grandfathered status.

25. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathered system identity is undefined.** The text does not determine when resumed training, architecture changes, new checkpoints, fine-tuning, or derivative models become a new system. Developers could characterize substantially new projects as continuations of exempt ones.

26. **§ 3(b)—No grandfathering documentation or verification is required.** There is no mandatory filing, contemporaneous recordkeeping requirement, or verification process establishing when training began and which system qualifies. Unsupported or difficult-to-disprove exemption claims could obstruct enforcement.

27. **§ 3(c)—The safety exception is effectively unbounded.** Any otherwise prohibited activity can claim exemption if conducted “for the purpose of safety evaluation,” without authorization, independence, or a defined evaluation standard. That could encompass training or deploying the very systems the bill otherwise prohibits.

28. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are not addressed.** The text does not require safety evaluation to be the exclusive or predominant purpose. A commercial development program could include some safety testing and argue that the broader program qualifies.

29. **§ 3(c)—No containment or scope limits apply to evaluation.** There are no compute limits, access controls, duration limits, restrictions on public deployment or weight release, or requirements to terminate unsafe experiments. Even genuine evaluation could therefore create the prohibited risks.

30. **§ 3(c)—No oversight or evidentiary requirements accompany the exception.** Evaluators need not register, retain records, report findings, or obtain approval, and no authority is expressly given to suspend an unsafe evaluation. The statute also leaves unresolved how an asserted safety purpose must be substantiated.

31. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** The bill supplies no performance specifications or treatment of general-purpose processors, custom accelerators, or alternative computing architectures. Operators could dispute which devices count toward facility coverage.

32. **§ 2(3)—Chip count is a poor and easily outdated proxy for capability.** Facilities with exactly 50,000 qualifying chips are excluded, as are smaller facilities with sufficiently powerful chips. No authority is provided to update the threshold or replace it with a compute-capacity standard.

33. **§§ 2(3), 4—Distributed facilities can avoid registration.** A project could distribute workloads across multiple data centers below the threshold while collectively using enormous compute. There is no aggregation rule for interconnected sites, common ownership, coordinated workloads, or cloud allocations.

34. **§§ 2(3), 4(a)—Facility boundaries and responsible operators are unclear.** “Data center” and “operator” are undefined, leaving uncertainty for multi-building campuses, colocation facilities, leased equipment, and layered cloud-service arrangements. The bill does not allocate reporting duties among owners, hosts, tenants, and workload controllers.

35. **§ 4(a)—The registry’s geographic scope is unspecified.** Unlike § 3, § 4 contains no express territorial or nationality rule. Its application to foreign facilities, including those controlled by U.S. entities, is consequently uncertain.

36. **§ 4(a)—Registration lacks deadlines and essential contents.** The bill does not say when existing or newly qualifying facilities must register, what information they must supply, or when they must update it. This makes timely compliance and violation findings harder to establish.

37. **§ 4(b)—Workload reports need not contain enforcement-critical information.** “Describing the computing workloads” does not expressly require customer identities, per-project compute, cross-facility identifiers, training start dates, model lineage, or claimed exemptions. Reports could be technically responsive yet insufficient to detect prohibited activity.

38. **§ 4(b)—Quarterly reporting is too delayed for rapid intervention.** A covered training project could begin and finish between reports, and no submission deadline after each quarter is specified. There is no advance notification or immediate reporting requirement for suspected prohibited activity.

39. **§ 4(b)—Self-certification lacks verification safeguards.** The statute requires no independent audits, underlying log retention, accuracy standard, or designation of an accountable certifying officer. Operators may also lack visibility into tenants’ workloads unless separately required to collect the necessary information.

40. **§§ 4, 5—Registry violations have no express statutory penalty.** Section 5 penalizes violations of § 3 only, not failures to register or report under § 4. Other law may address some false statements, but that does not establish a clear penalty for every reporting omission or nonregistration.

41. **§§ 3–5—Enforcement responsibilities and investigative powers are not specified.** No agency is expressly assigned overall enforcement responsibility or given tailored authority to compel records, inspect facilities, or test systems. Existing authorities may help, but their coverage should not be assumed.

42. **§ 5(a)—Civil enforcement procedures are missing.** The bill does not say who assesses penalties, whether enforcement proceeds administratively or in court, or how notice, hearings, review, and collection work. An administrative route would also need to account for constitutional constraints on agency adjudication of punitive civil penalties.

43. **§§ 3–5—No express preventive remedies are provided.** Penalties alone do not establish a clear mechanism for emergency stop orders, injunctions, disabling access, or securing covered model weights. The bill should not leave the availability and scope of urgent relief to litigation over other authorities.

44. **§ 5(a)—The penalty unit is ambiguous and may underdeter.** “For each day on which the violation occurs” does not clearly distinguish multiple projects, systems, or acts occurring on the same day, or define when an ongoing violation ends. The cap is unrelated to company revenue or project expenditure and could be treated as a business cost.

45. **§ 5—Liability standards need greater precision.** The civil provision specifies no mental-state requirement, while “willfully” in the criminal provision leaves questions about what the defendant must know regarding prohibited conduct, coverage, and legal duties. These uncertainties are particularly consequential for cloud providers and actors relying on exemption claims.

46. **§§ 5(a), 8—Penalty applicability conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5(a) reaches violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. Because § 3 is not yet effective during that interval, the text invites disputes over whether pre-effective-date conduct is punishable and raises retroactivity and fair-notice concerns.

47. **§§ 3(b), 8—The transition period is internally awkward.** Systems started between enactment and effectiveness are not grandfathered, but training during that period is not clearly prohibited. Companies could accelerate training and releases during the 180-day window, with no express transition, inventory, or shutdown obligations.

48. **§ 6—The international obligation is weak and ambiguous.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly require talks to begin or conclude by that deadline, much less produce an agreement. There are no participation requirements, verification standards, enforcement provisions, or reporting duties, and § 3’s loopholes would carry into an agreement requiring merely “equivalent” prohibitions.

49. **§ 7(a)—The safety finding lacks substantive and procedural standards.** The bill specifies neither who commissions the National Academies report nor its timing, methodology, or required conclusions. “Can be developed safely” could be satisfied by the existence of one safe development method without showing that unrestricted development or deployment is safe.

50. **§ 7(a)—The termination mechanism should expressly require enactment.** A joint resolution ordinarily must pass both houses and be presented to the President; “Congress … finds by joint resolution” should not suggest otherwise. If intended to permit termination without presentment, it would face a serious constitutional objection.

51. **§ 7(b)—The unconditional sunset defeats the safety condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years even if Congress never makes the finding required by § 7(a). The prohibition therefore does not actually persist until covered systems can be developed safely.

52. **§§ 7(a)–(b), 8—Expiration dates and residual obligations are unclear.** The ten-year clock begins at enactment despite the 180-day delay, while termination under § 7(a) expressly affects only the prohibition and could leave registry duties running. Although general savings law may preserve accrued penalties, an express transition provision should address pending cases, investigations, records, and outstanding orders.

53. **Act generally—No express implementation authority or dedicated resources.** The bill authorizes no implementing regulations and provides no dedicated funding or staffing for a technically demanding registry, evaluation, and enforcement program. Existing authority and appropriations might support some work, but leaving this implicit creates avoidable implementation risk.

54. **Act generally—No severability provision.** A successful challenge to the capability standard, a penalty mechanism, or another provision could generate disputes over how much of the remaining Act survives. Severability is not guaranteed or defeated by silence, but an express clause would better protect the intended remainder.
